## Inside the sandbox

[Section titled “Inside the sandbox”](#inside-the-sandbox)

These commands run inside a task’s sandbox. The runner and the workspace config start them; you don’t run them yourself.

### `gritz driver`

[Section titled “gritz driver”](#gritz-driver)

The driver server, which the runner’s backend starts in each sandbox. It runs the setup commands and the agent, and ships the task’s log.

| Flag                    | Default |                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--addr`                | `:8080` | The TCP address or `unix:///path` to serve on.                                                                      |
| `--prefix`              | `/`     | A directory prepended to every path the driver uses in the sandbox.                                                 |
| `--aws-lambda-hooks`    | off     | Also answer the Lambda MicroVM lifecycle hooks.                                                                     |
| `--aws-lambda-validate` |         | An executable to run on the Lambda MicroVM image’s validate hook, to warm the snapshot. Needs `--aws-lambda-hooks`. |

### `gritz tool agent-mcp`

[Section titled “gritz tool agent-mcp”](#gritz-tool-agent-mcp)

The MCP server behind the [agent tools](/using/agent-tools/). The runner adds it to every agent’s MCP config.

| Flag                |                                                                                              |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--task`, `-t`      | The task ID. Required.                                                                       |
| `--runner`, `-r`    | The runner ID. Required.                                                                     |
| `--workspace`, `-w` | The workspace. Required.                                                                     |
| `--token`           | The task’s token. Required.                                                                  |
| `--server`, `-s`    | The server URL. Defaults to `https://gritz.dev`.                                             |
| `--capability`      | A [capability](/operators/workspaces-yaml/#capabilities) of the task. Repeat it for several. |

### `gritz tool github-mcp`

[Section titled “gritz tool github-mcp”](#gritz-tool-github-mcp)

An MCP server over stdio that forwards to GitHub’s MCP server with GitHub App installation tokens, rotating them before they expire. For workspaces with the `github_token` capability; see [GitHub credentials for agents](/integrations/github/#github-credentials-for-agents).

| Flag        | Environment    | Default                              |                                                                     |
| ----------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--server`  | `GRITZ_SERVER` | `https://gritz.dev`                  | The server URL.                                                     |
| `--token`   | `GRITZ_TOKEN`  |                                      | The task’s token.                                                   |
| `--url`     |                | `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/` | GitHub’s MCP endpoint.                                              |
| `--min-ttl` |                | `5m`                                 | Rotate to a new token when the current one has less than this left. |

### Hidden commands

[Section titled “Hidden commands”](#hidden-commands)

`gritz --help` doesn’t list these two:

* `gritz tool git-credential`: a git credential helper that answers with GitHub App installation tokens, for workspaces with the `github_token` capability. It takes `--server` (`GRITZ_SERVER`) and `--token` (`GRITZ_TOKEN`). Configure it with `git config --global credential.https://github.com.helper "!gritz tool git-credential"`.
* `gritz tool proxy --addr <addr>`: connects its stdin and stdout to a TCP address or `unix:///path`. The Docker backend uses it to reach the driver’s socket.

# Custom event envelope

> The request and response of POST /webhook/custom, with every field, its validation, authentication and status codes.

The custom events webhook accepts one event per request. The [custom events guide](/integrations/custom-events/) shows how to set it up; this page is the precise contract.

## Request

[Section titled “Request”](#request)

```plaintext
POST /webhook/custom
Authorization: Bearer xat_…
Content-Type: application/json
```

The full URL is on **Settings → Organisation**, in the **Custom Events** card; for gritz.dev it is `https://gritz.dev/webhook/custom`. The webhook only handles `POST`.

### Authentication

[Section titled “Authentication”](#authentication)

* The request must carry `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A request without it gets `401 bearer token required`, even from a browser with a signed-in session: the webhook doesn’t accept session cookies.
* The token is an API key (`xat_…`) from the **Keys** page. A wrong, deleted or expired key gets `401 invalid or expired token`.
* The token must hold the `event:create` scope, or the request gets `403 permission denied`. API keys hold every scope. A task’s own token does not hold `event:create`.
* The event belongs to the key’s organisation and is checked against that organisation’s custom event types. It has no actor, so only the organisation’s public routing rules can match it.

### Body

[Section titled “Body”](#body)

A JSON object of at most 1 MiB:

```json
{
  "type": "alert",
  "url": "https://alerts.example.com/alerts/4211",
  "body": "checkout-api error rate above 5% for 10 minutes",
  "attrs": {"severity": ["critical"], "service": ["checkout-api"]},
  "details": {"runbook": "https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/checkout-api"}
}
```

Fields other than the five below are rejected, as are fields of the wrong JSON type.

| Field     | Type                                | Required | Validation                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------- | ----------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `type`    | string                              | yes      | Must name one of the organisation’s custom event types, as defined on **Events → Custom Schemas**. A type named like a built-in GitHub or Jira type still only resolves to the custom one. |
| `url`     | string                              | yes      | Must be non-empty and an absolute `http` or `https` URL with a host. Only GitHub and Jira URLs are normalised: see [`url`](#url).                                                          |
| `body`    | string                              | no       | The event’s text. Defaults to the empty string.                                                                                                                                            |
| `attrs`   | object of string → array of strings | no       | Every key must be an attribute the type declares, other than `body` and `url`.                                                                                                             |
| `details` | object of string → string           | no       | Not validated.                                                                                                                                                                             |

#### `type`

[Section titled “type”](#type)

The custom type’s name, which matches `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`. The type’s label becomes the event’s description on the task’s timeline.

#### `url`

[Section titled “url”](#url)

The resource the event is about, and the key that routes it: an event wakes the tasks subscribed to its `url`, and a task created by the event is subscribed to it.

gritz normalises GitHub and Jira issue URLs to one key per issue, as it does for their native events, so a custom event about a GitHub pull request or a Jira issue wakes the task subscribed to it:

| `url`                                                                                                                       | Key                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pull/{n}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment            | `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pull/{n}` |
| `https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pulls/{n}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment | `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pull/{n}` |
| `https://{site}.atlassian.net/browse/{KEY}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment                              | `https://{site}.atlassian.net/browse/{KEY}`                   |
| `https://{site}.atlassian.net/rest/api/{version}/issue/{KEY}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment            | `https://{site}.atlassian.net/browse/{KEY}`                   |

The host must match exactly (`github.com`, not `www.github.com`), and the key always uses `https`. A Jira REST URL with a numeric issue id instead of a key, and a GitHub API comment URL (`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/comments/{id}`), are not normalised.

Every other URL is used exactly as sent, so events about the same resource must send the same URL byte for byte.

#### `body`

[Section titled “body”](#body-1)

The event’s text, passed to the agent. Rules match on it through the `body` attribute every custom type declares.

#### `attrs`

[Section titled “attrs”](#attrs)

The values routing rule conditions match on, keyed by attribute. Each value is a list of strings; a condition matches when any value in the list satisfies it. An attribute the type declares may be omitted, in which case conditions on it don’t match. Sending `body` or `url` here is an error: send them as the top-level fields, from which their attributes are derived.

#### `details`

[Section titled “details”](#details)

Free-form key/value strings stored with the event and shown with it to the agent and in the Web UI. Rules can’t match on them.

## Response

[Section titled “Response”](#response)

A valid event gets `200 OK` with a JSON body:

```json
{"routed": 1}
```

`routed` is the number of tasks the event was delivered to: tasks created by the matching rule, or existing tasks subscribed to the event’s `url`. It is `0` when no public rule for the type matches, or when a rule matches but no task is subscribed to the `url` and the rule doesn’t create tasks.

Errors are plain text.

## Status codes

[Section titled “Status codes”](#status-codes)

| Status | Body                                                | Cause                                                                                                                               |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200`  | `{"routed": n}`                                     | The event was valid and routed to `n` tasks, possibly none.                                                                         |
| `400`  | `invalid envelope: …`                               | The body is not a JSON object matching the envelope: invalid JSON, an unknown field, a field of the wrong type, or more than 1 MiB. |
| `400`  | `unknown event type "…"`                            | `type` is empty or not one of the organisation’s custom types.                                                                      |
| `400`  | `url is required`                                   | `url` is missing or empty.                                                                                                          |
| `400`  | `url "…" must be an absolute http or https URL`     | `url` is relative, has no host, or has another scheme.                                                                              |
| `400`  | `attr "…" must be sent as the envelope's "…" field` | `attrs` has a `body` or `url` key.                                                                                                  |
| `400`  | `attr "…" not declared by event type "…"`           | `attrs` has a key the type doesn’t declare.                                                                                         |
| `401`  | `bearer token required`                             | No `Authorization: Bearer` header.                                                                                                  |
| `401`  | `invalid or expired token`                          | The bearer token is not a valid, unexpired API key or gritz token.                                                                  |
| `403`  | `permission denied`                                 | The token lacks the `event:create` scope.                                                                                           |
| `500`  | `internal error`                                    | The server failed to load the custom types or to route the event.                                                                   |

# Event types

> Every built-in GitHub and Jira event type, with its source and type, its label in the Web UI, and the attributes routing rule conditions can match.

Every event has a source and a type, such as `github` and `issue_comment`. A [routing rule](/concepts/routing-rules/) matches one `(source, type)` pair, which the rule form’s **Event type** list shows by its label, such as **GitHub: Issue/PR Comment**. Its conditions then test the event’s attributes.

This page lists the built-in types, from the [GitHub](/integrations/github/) and [Jira](/integrations/jira/) integrations. An organisation’s own types have the source `custom` and the attributes their schema defines; see [Custom events](/integrations/custom-events/).

## Attributes

[Section titled “Attributes”](#attributes)

Every type has two attributes:

* `body`: the event’s text, such as a comment. Its meaning depends on the type, and it is empty for types that have no text.
* `url`: the URL of what the event is about, such as a comment or an issue.

Each type adds others. An attribute can hold several values, such as every user mentioned in a comment, and a condition holds if any of them satisfies it. Conditions compare exactly and are case-sensitive; see [Matching](/concepts/routing-rules/#matching).

The **Label** column is what the rule form shows for the attribute.

## GitHub

[Section titled “GitHub”](#github)

Source `github`. GitHub usernames are given without the leading `@`.

### `issue_comment`

[Section titled “issue_comment”](#issue_comment)

**GitHub: Issue/PR Comment.** A comment on an issue or a pull request is created or edited.

| Attribute | Label        | Value                                                                                   |
| --------- | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Comment Body | The comment’s text.                                                                     |
| `url`     | Issue/PR URL | The comment’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/123#issuecomment-456`. |
| `mention` | Mention      | Each username @-mentioned in the comment.                                               |
| `user`    | User         | The username of the commenter.                                                          |

### `pull_request_review_comment`

[Section titled “pull_request_review_comment”](#pull_request_review_comment)

**GitHub: PR Review Comment.** An inline review comment on a pull request is created or edited.

| Attribute | Label               | Value                                                                                       |
| --------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Review Comment Body | The review comment’s text.                                                                  |
| `url`     | PR URL              | The review comment’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123#discussion_r456`. |
| `mention` | Mention             | Each username @-mentioned in the review comment.                                            |
| `user`    | User                | The username of the reviewer.                                                               |

The event also carries, for the agent but not for conditions, the file and line the comment is on (`path`, `line`, `start_line`, `side`) and its `diff_hunk`.

### `pull_request_review`

[Section titled “pull_request_review”](#pull_request_review)

**GitHub: PR Review.** A review with a summary is submitted on a pull request.

| Attribute | Label       | Value                                                                                     |
| --------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Review Body | The review’s summary.                                                                     |
| `url`     | PR URL      | The review’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123#pullrequestreview-456`. |
| `mention` | Mention     | Each username @-mentioned in the summary.                                                 |
| `user`    | User        | The username of the reviewer.                                                             |

### `issue_assigned`

[Section titled “issue_assigned”](#issue_assigned)

**GitHub: Issue Assigned.** An issue is assigned to someone.

| Attribute  | Label      | Value                                                                |
| ---------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`     | Issue Body | Empty.                                                               |
| `url`      | Issue URL  | The issue’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/123`. |
| `assignee` | Assignee   | The username newly assigned.                                         |
| `user`     | User       | The username of who assigned it.                                     |

### `pull_request_assigned`

[Section titled “pull_request_assigned”](#pull_request_assigned)

**GitHub: PR Assigned.** A pull request is assigned to someone.

| Attribute  | Label    | Value                                                                     |
| ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`     | PR Body  | Empty.                                                                    |
| `url`      | PR URL   | The pull request’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123`. |
| `assignee` | Assignee | The username newly assigned.                                              |
| `user`     | User     | The username of who assigned it.                                          |

### `pull_request_opened`

[Section titled “pull_request_opened”](#pull_request_opened)

**GitHub: PR Opened.** A pull request is opened.

| Attribute | Label          | Value                          |
| --------- | -------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `body`    | PR Description | Empty.                         |
| `url`     | PR URL         | The pull request’s URL.        |
| `user`    | User           | The username of who opened it. |

### `pull_request_closed`

[Section titled “pull_request_closed”](#pull_request_closed)

**GitHub: PR Closed.** A pull request is closed, with or without merging.

| Attribute | Label          | Value                                          |
| --------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | PR Description | `merged` or `closed`, as `state`.              |
| `url`     | PR URL         | The pull request’s URL.                        |
| `state`   | State          | `merged` if it was merged, otherwise `closed`. |
| `user`    | User           | The username of who closed or merged it.       |

### `label_added`

[Section titled “label_added”](#label_added)

**GitHub: Label Added.** A label is added to an issue or a pull request. Adding several labels sends one event per label.

| Attribute | Label         | Value                              |
| --------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Issue/PR Body | Empty.                             |
| `url`     | Issue/PR URL  | The issue’s or pull request’s URL. |
| `label`   | Label         | The label added.                   |
| `user`    | User          | The username of who added it.      |

## Jira

[Section titled “Jira”](#jira)

Source `atlassian`. People are identified by their Atlassian account ID, such as `5b10ac8d82e05b22cc7d4ef5`. Enter the bare ID, not the `[~accountid:…]` form Jira uses in comment text.

### `comment_created`

[Section titled “comment_created”](#comment_created)

**Jira: Issue Comment.** A comment is added to an issue.

| Attribute | Label        | Value                                                                                                  |
| --------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `body`    | Comment Body | The comment’s text.                                                                                    |
| `url`     | Issue URL    | The comment’s URL, such as `https://your-domain.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-123?focusedCommentId=10001`. |
| `mention` | Mention      | The account ID of each person @-mentioned in the comment.                                              |
| `user`    | User         | The account ID of the commenter.                                                                       |

### `label_added`

[Section titled “label_added”](#label_added-1)

**Jira: Label Added.** One or more labels are added to an issue. Adding several at once sends one event with all of them.

| Attribute | Label             | Value                                                                         |
| --------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Issue Description | Empty.                                                                        |
| `url`     | Issue URL         | The issue’s URL, such as `https://your-domain.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-123`. |
| `label`   | Label             | Each label added.                                                             |
| `user`    | User              | The account ID of who added them.                                             |

### `issue_assigned`

[Section titled “issue_assigned”](#issue_assigned-1)

**Jira: Issue Assigned.** An issue is assigned to someone.

| Attribute  | Label             | Value                               |
| ---------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `body`     | Issue Description | Empty.                              |
| `url`      | Issue URL         | The issue’s URL.                    |
| `assignee` | Assignee          | The account ID of the new assignee. |
| `user`     | User              | The account ID of who assigned it.  |

## URLs and subscriptions

[Section titled “URLs and subscriptions”](#urls-and-subscriptions)

The `url` attribute is the event’s own URL, as listed above, so a `url` condition sees the comment’s or review’s URL, with its fragment or query string. Use `prefix` to scope a rule to a repository or a project: `url prefix https://github.com/owner/repo/` or `url prefix https://your-domain.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-`.

To find subscribed tasks, gritz reduces the URL to the issue or pull request it belongs to, so an event about a comment reaches the tasks subscribed to its issue. See [Subscriptions](/concepts/events-and-links/#subscriptions).

# Agent tools

> The gritz tools every agent gets (get_my_task, update_my_task, create_link, report and get_github_token), what gritz tells agents to do with them, and how to write instructions that use them.

gritz adds an MCP server named `gritz` to every agent it runs, alongside the MCP servers in the task’s [workspace](/concepts/workspaces/). Its tools let the agent read and update its own task, and nothing else: they work with a token that only grants access to that task (see [Task tokens](/concepts/orgs-members-keys/#task-tokens)).

## What agents are told

[Section titled “What agents are told”](#what-agents-are-told)

On a task’s first run, before your instructions, gritz tells the agent to:

* name the task with `update_my_task` if it has no name;
* create a link with `subscribe=true` for each resource it creates, such as a pull request, an issue or a comment, so replies reach the task even after it finishes, and `subscribe=false` for reference links it didn’t create;
* prefer URLs a person can open over API URLs;
* use `report` for anything you should see, since its text replies aren’t shown;
* answer questions or problems on the platform the latest instruction or event came from, such as the pull request, and say which task it is from;
* call `get_my_task` if it needs to check for updates mid-run.

Then it gives the agent the task: its instructions, events and links, so it doesn’t need a tool call to start. On later runs the agent gets only what is new. See [Instructions and runs](/concepts/tasks/#instructions-and-runs).

## Tools

[Section titled “Tools”](#tools)

### `get_my_task`

[Section titled “get_my_task”](#get_my_task)

Returns the task: its ID, name, status, workspace, [namespace](/concepts/namespaces/) and URL, its links, and its instructions and events in order. Reports and status changes aren’t included.

### `update_my_task`

[Section titled “update_my_task”](#update_my_task)

Renames the task. It takes `name`, the new name. Agents can’t change anything else about their task, including its auto-archive delay.

### `create_link`

[Section titled “create_link”](#create_link)

Links the task to an external resource, and appears on the task’s timeline and in its sidebar.

| Parameter   |                                                                           |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`       | The resource’s URL.                                                       |
| `relevance` | How the resource relates to the task, such as “PR implementing the fix”.  |
| `title`     | Optional. A title to show for the link.                                   |
| `subscribe` | Optional. `true` to have events about the resource delivered to the task. |

A subscribed link is how a task hears about review comments on its pull request, or replies on its Jira issue. Which events wake it is up to the organisation’s [routing rules](/concepts/routing-rules/). See [Events and links](/concepts/events-and-links/).

### `report`

[Section titled “report”](#report)

Posts `message` to the task’s timeline. This is how an agent tells you what it did, what it found or what is blocking it: the agent’s own replies only appear in the task’s log.

### `get_github_token`

[Section titled “get_github_token”](#get_github_token)

Meant to return a short-lived GitHub token for the organisation’s GitHub App installation. Only tasks whose workspace has the `github_token` [capability](/operators/workspaces-yaml/#capabilities) get this tool, and the server doesn’t issue these tokens yet, so the tool always fails.

Agents get GitHub access today from their workspace instead: a token under `secrets:`, such as `GH_TOKEN`, which `gh`, git and the GitHub MCP server can use. See [`secrets`](/operators/secrets/).

## Writing instructions that use them

[Section titled “Writing instructions that use them”](#writing-instructions-that-use-them)

The agent already uses these tools as above without being asked. Mention them when you want something specific:

* **To get a summary where you’ll see it**: “When you’re done, report a summary of the changes and anything you couldn’t do.”
* **To keep a task listening**: “Open a draft pull request and link it with subscribe=true.” The task finishes, and a review comment on the pull request wakes it if a routing rule matches.
* **To link context you gave it**: “Link the incident page as a reference, not subscribed.”
* **To name it predictably**: “Name this task `deps: bump <package>`.”

The agent’s other tools, such as for GitHub or Jira, come from the MCP servers and credentials in its workspace. Ask your operator what a workspace provides, or see [`workspaces.yaml`](/operators/workspaces-yaml/).

# CLI

> Use the gritz CLI to create, list and update tasks, read a task's log, open a shell in its sandbox and get desktop notifications, and configure its server and API key.

The `gritz` binary is the CLI as well as the runner and server. Release binaries for Linux are attached to each [GitHub release](https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/releases); to build it from a checkout, run `mise run install`.

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

The CLI authenticates with an [API key](/concepts/orgs-members-keys/#api-keys), and acts in the organisation the key belongs to. Create one on the **Keys** page and save it in `config.json` in the gritz config directory:

```json
{
  "token": "xat_..."
}
```

The config directory is `GRITZ_CONFIG_DIR` if set, otherwise `gritz` under your user config directory: `~/.config/gritz` on Linux, `~/Library/Application Support/gritz` on macOS. A [runner](/operators/runner/) on the same machine reads the same file.

Every command talks to `https://gritz.dev` unless `--server` (`-s`) or the `GRITZ_SERVER` environment variable names another server:

```bash
export GRITZ_SERVER=https://gritz.example.com
```

`gritz notify` and `gritz mcp` are different: they take the key from `--token` or `GRITZ_TOKEN` rather than `config.json`, and the server only from `--server`.

## Tasks

[Section titled “Tasks”](#tasks)

### `gritz task create`

[Section titled “gritz task create”](#gritz-task-create)

Creates a task and starts it straight away, then prints it as JSON.

```bash
gritz task create -r my-runner -w pets-workshop \
  -i "Add a --json flag to the list command and open a pull request."
```

| Flag                  |                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--runner`, `-r`      | The [runner](/concepts/runners/) to run on. Required.                                                                                                                  |
| `--workspace`, `-w`   | The [workspace](/concepts/workspaces/). Defaults to `default`.                                                                                                         |
| `--instruction`, `-i` | An instruction. Repeat it for several.                                                                                                                                 |
| `--name`, `-n`        | The task’s name. The agent names it if you don’t.                                                                                                                      |
| `--auto-archive`      | The [auto-archive](/concepts/tasks/#auto-archive) delay, such as `1h` or `24h`. `0`, the default, is never; a negative value archives the task as soon as it finishes. |

The **Workspaces** page in the Web UI lists runner IDs and their workspaces.

### `gritz task list`

[Section titled “gritz task list”](#gritz-task-list)

Prints the organisation’s 50 newest unarchived tasks as JSON, with their status, runner, workspace and URL.

### `gritz task update`

[Section titled “gritz task update”](#gritz-task-update)

Changes a task.

```bash
gritz task update 1234 --start -i "Also update the README."
```

| Flag                      |                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--add-instruction`, `-i` | Add an instruction. Repeat it for several.                                                                                                  |
| `--start`, `-r`           | Start the task, as the Web UI does when you send an instruction. A running task isn’t interrupted: it runs again when its current run ends. |
| `--name`, `-n`            | Rename the task.                                                                                                                            |
| `--auto-archive`          | Set the auto-archive delay.                                                                                                                 |

An instruction added without `--start` waits on the task until something else starts it, such as an event or a later `--start`.

Every `gritz task update` also sets the task’s auto-archive delay: to `--auto-archive` when it is given, and otherwise to never. Pass `--auto-archive` again to keep a delay the task already had.

Cancelling, restarting and archiving tasks are done in the [Web UI](/using/web-ui/#the-task-page).

## `gritz logs`

[Section titled “gritz logs”](#gritz-logs)

Prints a task’s log: the setup commands, the agent’s output and gritz’s own lines, as the Web UI’s **Logs** view shows them. It works for any task in the organisation, including tasks whose sandbox is gone.

```bash
gritz logs 1234     # print the log so far
gritz logs -f 1234  # and keep following it
```

`--interval` sets how often `-f` checks for new output, `2s` by default.

## `gritz shell`

[Section titled “gritz shell”](#gritz-shell)

Opens an interactive shell in a finished task’s sandbox, to look at what the agent left behind:

```bash
gritz shell 1234
```

The runner starts the sandbox again with a shell in place of the agent. It works whatever the runner’s backend and wherever it runs: the server relays the session, so you need no access to the runner. See [A shell in the sandbox](/operators/debugging/#a-shell-in-the-sandbox).

## `gritz notify`

[Section titled “gritz notify”](#gritz-notify)

Stays running and shows a desktop notification each time one of the organisation’s tasks completes, fails or is cancelled.

```bash
GRITZ_TOKEN=xat_... gritz notify
```

`--title` sets the notifications’ title, `gritz` by default. It uses `notify-send` on Linux and the system notifications on macOS and Windows.

## Other commands

[Section titled “Other commands”](#other-commands)

* `gritz mcp` runs a local MCP server that lets Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients create and manage tasks; see [MCP](/integrations/mcp/).
* `gritz runner`, `gritz download`, `gritz workspaces` and `gritz containers` are for running a runner; see [Runner](/operators/runner/) and [Debugging](/operators/debugging/).
* `gritz version` prints the CLI’s version.

[CLI reference](/reference/cli/) lists every command and flag.

# Web UI

> A tour of the gritz Web UI, the task list and task page, schedules, events and routing rules, workspaces, members, keys and settings.

The Web UI is served by the gritz server under `/ui/`, for example `https://gritz.dev/ui/`. It updates live: task statuses, timelines and logs change as they happen, without reloading. The dot next to the organisation selector shows whether the live connection is up.

The bar at the top links to every page, and holds the organisation selector, the light and dark theme toggle, **Settings** and **Logout**. Press Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac) anywhere to jump to a task by name.

## Tasks

[Section titled “Tasks”](#tasks)

**Tasks** lists the organisation’s tasks, newest first, with their runner, workspace and [status](/concepts/tasks/#statuses). A `command:` badge next to the status is an action the runner hasn’t carried out yet. Turn on **Show archived** to include archived tasks, and archive or unarchive a task from its row.

**+ Task** creates a task. Pick a runner, then one of its workspaces; the name, [namespace](/concepts/namespaces/) and [auto-archive](/concepts/tasks/#auto-archive) delay are optional. The form remembers the last runner and workspace you used. The task is created as a draft, and starts when you send its first instruction.

## The task page

[Section titled “The task page”](#the-task-page)

The sidebar on the left holds the task’s status and name, its three views, its details (runner, workspace, namespace, created and updated times), its links, and its actions:

* **Archive** or **Unarchive**. When an auto-archive delay is counting down, the time left shows next to it.
* **Cancel**, while the task is pending or running.
* **Restart**, once it is running or finished.
* **Auto-archive**, to change the delay: never, immediately, 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours or 7 days.

The arrow at the top collapses the sidebar to icons.

### Timeline

[Section titled “Timeline”](#timeline)

The timeline is everything that happened to the task, in order: your instructions, events from GitHub, Jira and custom sources, the agent’s reports, links it created, and status changes with who caused them. It opens at the latest entry and loads older ones as you scroll up.

The box at the bottom sends an instruction: Enter sends it, Shift+Enter adds a new line. A finished task starts again with it; a running task picks it up when its current run ends. See [Instructions and runs](/concepts/tasks/#instructions-and-runs).

### Logs

[Section titled “Logs”](#logs)

The task’s log, as the sandbox writes it: setup commands, the agent’s messages and tool calls, and gritz’s own lines. It follows new output while the task runs. Declared [secrets](/operators/secrets/) are masked.

### Shell

[Section titled “Shell”](#shell)

A terminal in the task’s sandbox, for looking at what the agent left behind. It can be opened once the task has finished, and works like [`gritz shell`](/using/cli/#gritz-shell): the runner starts the sandbox again with a shell in place of the agent.

## Schedules

[Section titled “Schedules”](#schedules)

**Schedules** lists the organisation’s [schedules](/concepts/schedules/) with their cron expression, timezone, next run and workspace, and the task each created last. From each row you can turn a schedule on or off, run it now, edit it or delete it. **+ Schedule** creates one.

## Events

[Section titled “Events”](#events)

**Events** has three tabs:

* **Routing Rules**: the organisation’s [routing rules](/concepts/routing-rules/), in the order they are checked, with their event type, conditions and action. Reorder them with the arrows, edit or remove them, add one with **+ Rule**, or try an event against them with **Test**.
* **Recent Events**: the latest events delivered to the organisation’s tasks. Open one to see its description, URL, data and the task it reached.
* **Custom Schemas**: the organisation’s custom event types. See [Custom events](/integrations/custom-events/).

## Workspaces

[Section titled “Workspaces”](#workspaces)

**Workspaces** lists the [workspaces](/concepts/workspaces/) the organisation’s [runners](/concepts/runners/) have registered, with their description, runner and when they were last registered. Filter by runner, and **Clear** to remove the listed runner’s workspaces, or every runner’s.

## Members and Keys

[Section titled “Members and Keys”](#members-and-keys)

**Members** lists the organisation’s members and their role. The owner adds members by email here and removes them. **Keys** lists the organisation’s API keys and creates and deletes them. See [Organisations, members and API keys](/concepts/orgs-members-keys/).

## Settings

[Section titled “Settings”](#settings)

**Settings** has two tabs:

* **Account**: the organisations you own, where you create new ones and delete them, and your linked [Atlassian](/integrations/jira/#link-your-atlassian-account) and [GitHub](/integrations/github/#link-your-github-account) accounts. Linking them lets [routing rules](/concepts/routing-rules/#public-rules) recognise your comments as a member’s.
* **Organisation**: the URLs and settings that connect the organisation to other systems: the [MCP server URL](/integrations/mcp/) for MCP clients, the [custom events](/integrations/custom-events/) webhook URL, the [GitHub App installation](/integrations/github/#install-the-github-app), and the [Atlassian webhook](/integrations/jira/#connect-jira) URL and secret.

The server’s version is at the bottom of the page.
